# project — how it is put together

*Generated by Shipyard on 2026-11-09. Regenerated when the project changes — edit the project, not this file.*

**What it is:** A café with eight part-time staff plans shifts in a group chat. Nobody is sure who is on when, swaps get agreed in private messages, and the manager finds out when somebody does not turn up.

Built for one small café: the manager plans the week in a few minutes, staff see only their own shifts on their phone, and a swap is asked for and approved in the app, so the manager always knows who is really working.

**How far it is going right now:** a working prototype for people the owner knows

## The stack

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Framework | Next.js |
| Language | TypeScript |
| Database | PostgreSQL, through Prisma |
| Tests | Vitest |

Shipyard carries its own Node and PostgreSQL, so neither needs installing.
That is also the reason the choice is not open: anything requiring a service
Shipyard does not ship cannot run on the owner’s machine.

## Where things live

```
src/app/           pages and API routes
src/components/    installed parts — do not edit inside these
src/lib/           shared code, including the database connection
prisma/schema.prisma   the database, as the code understands it
tests/contracts/   the tests that came with installed parts
```

In `prisma/schema.prisma`, everything between the two `shipyard:components`
markers was written by the installer. Your own tables go below them.

## How it gets built

1. **The first real feature** — One thing, finished properly: the screen first so you can see it, then everything behind it. It tells us the shape of the rest. _(Depends on how big that one feature is)_
2. **The rest of the features** — Each one finished before the next one starts, so the app is never half-broken. _(Depends on how many features there are)_
3. **Show it to someone** — A private link you can send. The information is real, and so is sign-in if your app has it, but nothing is backed up, so do not put anything in it you cannot lose. _(Shipyard puts it online for you)_

Each phase ends with something visible in the app. A phase that ends with
"the data model is complete" is one the owner cannot check, and a phase
the owner cannot check is one where progress and the appearance of
progress are the same thing.

## What has to be true before real people use it

The production checklist stands at **0 out of 100**. For a working prototype for people the owner knows that number is for reference: readiness is decided by the blocking checks below; from a customer pilot up it must also reach 40.

That number is scored against the whole production checklist rather than
against this project’s own obligations. A concept build genuinely scores
around 17, and that is correct — what changes with ambition is the bar, not
the yardstick. Scoring "percentage of what you owe" would let a concept
build score 100 and make the number meaningless.

Currently blocking:

- The one thing this build is for is showing that the main journey works. Until it builds and that journey runs end to end, there is nothing to show.

## What this deliberately does not do

- **An app in the App Store.** Anycreo cannot build this yet. Shipyard builds web apps, which work on a phone browser. A real App Store app needs a different toolchain and a developer account.
- **Live voice or video.** Anycreo cannot build this yet. This needs infrastructure Shipyard does not run yet. A scheduled call link from an existing tool is the usual stand-in.
- **A way for you to see what is going on.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **A record of who did what.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Signing in.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Somewhere for it to live on the internet.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Finding out when it breaks.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Keeping customers separate.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Who is allowed to do what.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Emailing your users.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a pilot with real people.
- **Knowing it is still up.** Not needed for a working prototype. It becomes necessary at a product people pay for.
- **Taking payment.** Nothing here charges anybody.
- **Holding sensitive personal information.** The project was set up on the basis that it does not. If that changes, the obligations change with it.
- **Being used by strangers.** This is not built to withstand that yet, and the checks that would prove it is have not been run.

This list is here on purpose. A document that says what a system does and
not what it will not do is why people spend a week discovering a limit that
was decided deliberately in week one.
